paragraphs: Constrained reinforcement learning asks an agent to improve its decisions while respecting limits on its behavior. This paper studies that problem using an average criterion, which evaluates performance over the long run. The authors argue that this criterion is often more suitable than discounting future outcomes, yet algorithms developed for discounted problems frequently perform poorly when adapted to the average setting.

Their proposed algorithm, Average-Constrained Policy Optimization, or ACPO, combines policy optimization with function approximation. Its design draws inspiration from trust region methods. To support the algorithm, the authors develop sensitivity theory for average constrained decision processes: mathematical bounds describing how changes affect performance. Those bounds then inform the optimization procedure.

The paper provides theoretical performance guarantees and evaluates ACPO in challenging OpenAI Gym environments. In those experiments, it performs better than other leading algorithms adapted to the average constrained setting. The contribution therefore connects analysis tailored to the average objective with an algorithm whose reported empirical advantages concern that same problem.
icml-2024-acpo-a-policy-optimization-alg.tldr: ACPO uses sensitivity bounds to optimize constrained reinforcement learning policies under a long-run average objective.

paragraphs: Models that predict something at every image pixel can be vulnerable to small input changes. Testing that vulnerability requires attacks that meaningfully challenge predictions across the image. Existing approaches can concentrate errors on isolated pixels, while attempts to distribute their effects more broadly can make optimization less stable and less efficient.

CosPGD addresses this trade-off by modifying how the attack loss is weighted. It computes an alignment score between each pixel-wise prediction and its target, then uses that score to scale the loss smoothly. Because this operation is fully differentiable, it fits into gradient-based attack optimization while encouraging errors to be spread more evenly across the image.

The method supports robustness evaluation for semantic segmentation and regression tasks, including optical flow, disparity estimation, and image restoration. The authors report improved attack efficiency and performance beyond the previous leading segmentation attack. Its significance is a shared attack mechanism that works with several forms of pixel-level output, rather than requiring a separate construction for each task.
icml-2024-cospgd-an-efficient-white-box-.tldr: CosPGD smoothly reweights pixel-level attack losses to produce more balanced errors and more efficient robustness evaluations.

paragraphs: A language model can be uncertain because it lacks knowledge or because the text itself allows multiple plausible continuations. The paper investigates whether these sources of uncertainty can be distinguished in free-form text. That distinction matters because additional knowledge could reduce the first kind, whereas variability in the underlying distribution remains even for a better-informed model.

The authors do not have ground-truth probabilities, so they use a substantially larger model as an approximate reference. They train small linear probes on representations from frozen pretrained models to predict when the larger model will be more confident about a token. These probes make accurate predictions and transfer across text domains. A fully unsupervised method also achieves non-trivial accuracy.

These findings support the authors’ interpretation that language models contain internal signals about different kinds of uncertainty. The conclusion remains approximate because greater confidence from a larger model stands in for ground truth. The results suggest a possible route toward more informative confidence indicators, rather than establishing a definitive separation of knowledge gaps from unavoidable uncertainty.
icml-2024-distinguishing-the-knowable-fr.tldr: Small probes can predict when a larger language model will be more confident, offering evidence of internal signals about uncertainty types.

paragraphs: Prediction-based neural architecture search depends on models that estimate how well candidate networks will perform. The representation given to those predictors strongly influences their usefulness. This paper examines that representation choice, moving beyond the traditional adjacency matrix that describes a network’s graph connections.

The authors organize encodings into three categories: structural descriptions, learned representations, and score-based vectors. They also introduce unified encodings that allow predictors to operate across multiple architecture search spaces. Their investigation covers more than 1.5 million architectures from several established spaces, providing a broad basis for studying how encoding and predictor design work together.

The resulting predictor, Flow Attention for NAS, or FLAN, combines lessons about architecture representations, transfer learning, and unified encodings. The authors report that it reduces the cost of training architecture accuracy predictors by more than an order of magnitude. This finding concerns the predictor-training stage of architecture search: better representations and reuse across spaces can make that supporting component substantially less expensive.
icml-2024-encodings-for-prediction-based.tldr: The paper studies architecture encodings and introduces FLAN, reducing NAS accuracy-predictor training costs by more than an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether Gaussian process regression can use less energy by performing calculations with lower-precision floating-point numbers. Lower precision changes how accurately numerical values are represented, so the central question is how much energy can be saved while maintaining the model’s predictive performance.

The authors study this question through the interaction of dataset properties, implementation choices, numerical precision, and energy consumption. Their key condition is that the kernel matrix is well-conditioned. This makes matrix conditioning central to interpreting the result: the reported energy savings come with a numerical property that supports reducing precision without substantially changing model performance.

Under that condition, the authors report energy reductions of up to 89.01% for 98.08% of arithmetic operations, with little or no effect on performance. These figures describe the reported arithmetic savings, rather than a universal reduction for every Gaussian process workload. The paper also identifies relevance beyond Gaussian processes wherever computation requires inversion of a symmetric full-rank matrix, connecting the study to a broader numerical operation.
icml-2024-energy-efficient-gaussian-proc.tldr: Low-precision arithmetic can substantially reduce Gaussian process regression energy use when the kernel matrix is well-conditioned.

paragraphs: A model’s accuracy across groups does not fully describe its biases. Two groups may have similar error rates while the model makes systematically different kinds of mistakes for each. This paper argues that evaluating spurious correlations requires examining the relationship between a bias attribute and the predictions involved in those errors.

The authors introduce SkewSize, a metric inspired by hypothesis testing. It aggregates effect sizes describing the interaction between a categorical bias variable and the model’s predicted category. This shifts attention from the number of mistakes to their structure. The metric supports multiclass prediction and can also be extended to generative models with open vocabularies.

The paper demonstrates SkewSize on vision models trained with synthetic data, ImageNet models, and vision-and-language models from the BLIP-2 family. Across these settings, it reveals biases missed by other metrics and offers insight into the effects of techniques such as instruction tuning. The contribution is a way to characterize error patterns that standard worst-group accuracy or accuracy-gap summaries can leave hidden.
icml-2024-evaluating-model-bias-requires.tldr: SkewSize detects model biases by measuring how prediction mistakes relate to bias attributes, revealing patterns that accuracy summaries can miss.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation lets a model adjust to distribution changes using unlabeled data encountered during deployment. More elaborate adaptation methods can improve predictions, but their extra computation takes time. The paper argues that evaluations which overlook this time cost can give an incomplete picture of how useful these methods will be in practice.

The proposed evaluation protocol supplies data as an online stream arriving at a constant speed. A slower method consequently receives fewer samples for adaptation. This makes adaptation speed part of the evaluation itself, linking the available learning opportunities to how quickly a method can process the stream.

The authors benchmark several methods across multiple datasets and scenarios. They find that simple, fast approaches can outperform more sophisticated, slower ones under this protocol; SHOT outperforming SAR is one reported example. The finding concerns performance under an explicit time constraint, showing that method rankings can change when computation affects access to adaptation data. It supports evaluating accuracy together with the speed needed to sustain it.
icml-2024-evaluation-of-test-time-adapta.tldr: Evaluating adaptation on a constant-speed data stream shows that faster, simpler methods can outperform slower, more sophisticated ones.

paragraphs: Graph-based machine learning builds relationships into a model’s structure, while Gaussian processes additionally provide a way to account for uncertainty. Ordinary graphs describe pairwise relationships between vertices. This paper extends Gaussian process modeling to settings where the relevant structure also includes interactions involving higher-order objects.

The proposed domain is a cellular complex, a generalization of a graph containing vertices, edges, and higher-order cells. Using this structure allows the model to represent relationships beyond pairs of vertices. The contribution therefore concerns both the objects over which a Gaussian process is defined and the structural information available to it.

The authors derive two kernels, which specify how the model relates values across that structure. One extends the graph Matérn kernel to cellular complexes. The other also mixes information between different cell types, allowing the model to connect information across structural levels. Together, these constructions expand uncertainty-aware modeling beyond the pairwise setting and give two distinct ways to incorporate the richer relationships supplied by cellular complexes.
icml-2024-gaussian-processes-on-cellular.tldr: The paper extends Gaussian processes to cellular complexes with kernels for higher-order relationships and information sharing across cell types.

paragraphs: Optimization methods that seek flat minima have achieved practical success, motivating a precise question: what should count as a flat minimum, and how difficult is it to find one? This paper formalizes flatness using the trace of the Hessian, a quantity that summarizes curvature of the objective, and defines an approximate flat minimum through that measure.

The authors then analyze a gradient-based algorithm for finding such points efficiently in general cost functions. Its central mechanism evaluates gradients at randomly perturbed versions of the current iterate. Those evaluations help estimate a direction leading toward flatter minima, giving random perturbations a specific role in the search for low-curvature solutions.

For empirical-risk objectives built from training data, the paper presents a faster algorithm inspired by sharpness-aware minimization. The analysis offers theoretical support for that practical approach under the paper’s definition of flatness. The contribution is therefore both a formal target for optimization and algorithms with efficiency analysis for reaching it, with an additional improvement for the training-data setting.
icml-2024-how-to-escape-sharp-minima-wit.tldr: Randomly perturbed gradient evaluations help algorithms find minima that are approximately flat under a Hessian-trace definition.

paragraphs: In singular statistical models, the Fisher information matrix is degenerate at the true parameter. The paper explains that fixed-step gradient descent can require a number of iterations growing polynomially with sample size to reach the final statistical neighborhood of that parameter. This motivates using local curvature to accelerate parameter estimation.

The authors analyze normalized gradient descent, or NormGD, whose step size is scaled using the largest eigenvalue of the empirical loss Hessian. Their analysis connects the idealized population loss to the loss computed from finite samples. That connection addresses the challenge posed by a sample loss that can be nonconvex.

When the population loss is homogeneous, NormGD reaches the final statistical radius in a number of iterations logarithmic in sample size. For fixed dimension, the authors report optimal computational complexity O(n), compared with O(n^τ) for fixed-step gradient descent, where τ exceeds one. These are conditional results: homogeneity and fixed dimension are central to the stated improvement, which concerns reaching statistical accuracy rather than exact recovery.
icml-2024-improving-computational-comple.tldr: Under homogeneous population loss and fixed dimension, curvature-scaled gradient descent reaches statistical accuracy with optimal O(n) computational complexity.

paragraphs: Studies of in-context learning often use synthetic tasks that differ substantially from language modeling. This paper introduces in-context language learning as a bridge: a model receives strings from a formal language and must generate more strings belonging to that language. The authors focus on regular languages produced by random finite automata.

Across these tasks, Transformers substantially outperform models with recurrent or convolutional representations. The authors provide evidence that specialized attention heads help Transformers compute in-context n-gram statistics, which describe patterns of short token sequences. This offers a candidate mechanism for the observed architectural advantage, connecting behavior on the task to identifiable computations.

The paper then builds these attention heads directly into neural models. This improves both synthetic language-learning performance and natural language modeling. On SlimPajama, the authors report perplexity reductions of up to 1.14 points, or 6.7%, for 340-million-parameter Transformers. The result shows how a controlled formal-language task can generate architectural insights that also prove useful in a natural-text setting.
icml-2024-in-context-language-learning-a.tldr: Formal-language learning tasks reveal evidence for n-gram attention mechanisms whose explicit inclusion also improves natural language modeling.

paragraphs: Many scientific sampling problems specify a distribution through an energy function without providing normalized probabilities or example samples. The paper introduces Iterated Denoising Energy Matching, or iDEM, to train a diffusion-based sampler using only that energy function and its gradient. This targets the challenge of efficiently producing statistically independent samples from such distributions.

Training alternates between drawing samples from regions where the current model places high density and using those samples in a stochastic score-matching objective to improve the sampler. The inner matching objective is simulation-free and does not require MCMC samples. The method also uses diffusion’s ability to mix between modes to smooth the energy landscape and support exploration.

Experiments span synthetic energy functions and invariant many-body particle systems. The authors report state-of-the-art results on all evaluated metrics and training that is two to five times faster. They also report the first energy-based training of a sampler for the challenging 55-particle Lennard-Jones system. These findings demonstrate the approach’s practical reach on the tested sampling problems.
icml-2024-iterated-denoising-energy-matc.tldr: iDEM trains diffusion samplers directly from energy functions and gradients, reporting faster training and strong results on demanding particle systems.

paragraphs: Position-based reweighting can help linearized Transformers retain model quality, but leading approaches rely on knowing sequence lengths. That creates a problem when output is generated incrementally or input arrives while output is being produced. In those settings, the final target length, and sometimes the input length, is unavailable.

LeaPformer addresses this dependency through Learned Proportions. First, it reformulates reweighting in terms of sequence proportions instead of explicit positions and lengths. Second, a compact module produces dynamic proportions in place of static position representations. This gives the model more flexible ways to concentrate attention while making the approach usable for autoregressive and simultaneous tasks.

On Long-Range Arena, LeaPformer achieves the best quality-throughput trade-off among the eight representative efficient Transformers used for comparison. The authors also report competitive results on Wikitext-103b autoregressive language modeling and simultaneous speech-to-text translation for two language pairs. These findings support the practicality of replacing length-dependent reweighting with learned proportions across the evaluated tasks.
icml-2024-leapformer-enabling-linear-tra.tldr: LeaPformer learns dynamic sequence proportions to support efficient attention when final sequence lengths are unknown.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering functional data generated by a mixture of Gaussian processes. The goal is to recover the hidden group associated with each observed function. Its approach turns that problem into a collection of simpler clustering problems and then combines their answers.

The key observation is that projecting a function onto a chosen projection function produces a coefficient following a one-dimensional Gaussian mixture model. The method repeats this operation with multiple projections and fits a separate mixture model to each set of coefficients. Each fitted model supplies one clustering, and ensemble clustering merges these into a consensus assignment. Multiple views therefore contribute to the final grouping.

The authors report a substantial computational reduction relative to leading methods and provide theoretical guarantees for identifying and learning Gaussian process mixtures. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets also favor the proposed approach over existing techniques. The contribution combines a distributional property of projections with ensemble clustering, making a potentially costly functional-data problem accessible through many simpler one-dimensional models.
icml-2024-learning-mixtures-of-gaussian-.tldr: The method clusters Gaussian-process-mixture data by combining Gaussian mixture clusterings from multiple one-dimensional projections.

paragraphs: Nonlinear filtering estimates the distribution of a changing hidden state from a history of noisy, partial observations. Conventional sequential importance resampling particle filters can struggle when their weights degenerate, particularly with high-dimensional states or degenerate likelihoods. This paper explores a different way to update the state distribution.

The method estimates a Brenier optimal transport map that moves the current prior distribution to the posterior at the next time step. Its formulation does not require an analytical expression for the likelihood. It also allows neural networks to approximate complex distributions, including distributions with multiple modes, and uses stochastic optimization to support scalability.

The authors compare the transport approach with a sequential importance resampling particle filter and an ensemble Kalman filter in extensive numerical experiments. The evaluation examines sample efficiency, scaling with state dimension, and representation of complex or multimodal distributions. The contribution is an alternative filtering construction that brings transport maps and neural approximation into the sequential update, with experiments directed at the difficulties motivating it.
icml-2024-nonlinear-filtering-with-breni.tldr: The paper uses learned Brenier transport maps to update filtering distributions without requiring an analytical likelihood.

paragraphs: Prediction uncertainty becomes harder to quantify when deployment data differs from training data. This paper separates two sources of change: the distribution of input variables and the relationship between inputs and outcomes. Treating these separately lets the method use information about one kind of shift while remaining cautious about the other.

The framework reweights training examples to correct an identifiable change in the input distribution. It then protects against worst-case changes in the conditional outcome distribution within a specified f-divergence ball. Combining conformal inference with distributionally robust learning produces approximately valid and efficient prediction intervals under this formulation.

The protection is tied to the stated structure: the input shift must be identifiable, and the conditional shift is bounded by the chosen uncertainty set. The authors also apply the framework to sensitivity analysis for individual treatment effects under hidden confounding. Simulations and four real-data applications show better robustness and efficiency than the evaluated benchmarks, supporting the value of distinguishing shift types when constructing uncertainty intervals.
icml-2024-not-all-distributional-shifts-.tldr: The framework adjusts identifiable input shifts and guards against bounded conditional shifts to construct approximately valid prediction intervals.

paragraphs: Powerful optimization solvers are difficult to use without expertise in translating practical problems into mathematical models. OptiMUS addresses that barrier with a language-model-based agent that takes natural-language descriptions of linear and mixed-integer linear programming problems. Its purpose is to carry the description through the modeling and solving process.

The agent develops a mathematical formulation, writes and debugs solver code, evaluates the resulting solutions, and uses those evaluations to improve both model and code. A modular structure lets it handle lengthy descriptions and complex data without relying on long prompts. The workflow therefore includes revision after evaluation, rather than ending with an initial formulation.

The authors report performance improvements over existing leading methods exceeding 20% on easy datasets and 30% on hard datasets. The hard evaluations include NLP4LP, a newly released dataset containing long and complex problems. These results support the usefulness of a modular, iterative agent for the evaluated optimization-modeling tasks, especially where substantial descriptions and data complicate the translation into solver-ready form.
icml-2024-optimus-scalable-optimization-.tldr: OptiMUS turns natural-language optimization problems into mathematical models and solver code, then evaluates and revises its solutions.

paragraphs: An average reward describes long-run performance but does not capture all of its variability. This paper uses asymptotic variance as a risk measure for average-reward reinforcement learning, motivated by safety-critical applications. It focuses on policy evaluation: estimating this risk for a policy, providing information that future policy-learning methods could use.

The authors derive a temporal-difference-style algorithm from a formulation of asymptotic variance involving the solution of a Poisson equation. They use linear stochastic approximation to turn that formulation into a sequential estimator. The analysis covers both tabular representations and linear function approximation, so the contribution includes two common ways of representing the quantities being estimated.

The paper establishes a finite-time convergence rate of approximately 1/k, with logarithmic factors suppressed, after k algorithm steps. The authors identify their result, to their knowledge, as the first sequential estimator of Markov-chain asymptotic variance with finite-sample guarantees. It also supplies a foundation for future actor-critic algorithms that constrain variance, rather than itself presenting the completed variance-constrained control method.
icml-2024-policy-evaluation-for-variance.tldr: A temporal-difference-style estimator evaluates asymptotic variance in average-reward reinforcement learning with finite-sample convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Fairness in a sequence of decisions can depend on what happened earlier and on how multiple stakeholders have been affected over time. The paper argues that fairness is therefore often non-Markovian: judging the current decision requires relevant history. It also emphasizes that fairness may need to hold during a process, rather than being assessed only after the final outcome.

The authors develop this perspective through notions of long-term, anytime, periodic, and bounded fairness. These distinguish different temporal requirements for assessing a decision process. They also study the connection between fairness and memory, examining how retaining information about earlier decisions can support the construction of fair policies.

The algorithmic contribution is FairQCM, a reinforcement learning method that automatically augments its training data to improve sample efficiency when synthesizing fair policies. Together, the framework and algorithm connect the specification of fairness over time with the information and learning process needed to support it. The central shift is to treat decision history as part of the fairness problem itself.
icml-2024-remembering-to-be-fair-non-mar.tldr: The paper formalizes history-dependent fairness and introduces FairQCM to improve sample efficiency when learning fair sequential policies.

paragraphs: This paper studies constrained min-max optimization problems that may be stochastic and nonconvex-nonconcave but satisfy particular structural conditions. Those conditions are cohypomonotonicity or a weak Minty variational inequality. A parameter ρ measures the permitted degree of nonconvexity, with larger values allowing more difficult problems.

Earlier guarantees required ρ to be less than 1/(2L), where L describes smoothness. The authors obtain optimal or best-known complexity guarantees under the broader condition ρ < 1/L, reaching a conjectured tolerance threshold for first-order methods. A key analytical tool is conic nonexpansiveness, an operator property used to improve the convergence arguments.

The paper also refines analysis of inexact Halpern iteration, relaxing how accurately its internal computations must be performed and improving some results even for constrained stochastic convex-concave problems. Finally, it analyzes stochastic inexact Krasnosel’skii-Mann iteration with a multilevel Monte Carlo estimator when the structural assumptions hold only relative to a solution. These advances broaden guarantees within specified structured classes, rather than covering unrestricted nonconvex min-max optimization.
icml-2024-revisiting-inexact-fixed-point.tldr: Sharper fixed-point analyses extend min-max convergence guarantees to greater structured nonconvexity and improve tolerance of inexact computations.

paragraphs: Flow and diffusion generative models construct a continuous-time transformation between a simple base distribution and a target distribution represented by data samples. Conventionally, the base is chosen without reference to the data. This paper studies how deliberately linking base samples to target samples can support conditional generation.

Using stochastic interpolants, the authors formalize couplings in which a base sample is computed conditionally on a target sample. This introduces dependence into the pair used to construct the transport map. It is a different mechanism from adding class labels or continuous embeddings, although the approaches can be used together. The resulting maps function as conditional generative models.

The authors show that these transport maps can be learned through a squared-loss regression problem analogous to the one used with independent base and target samples. Experiments in super-resolution and in-painting demonstrate the practical usefulness of dependent couplings. The contribution is a way to encode dependence directly into the transport construction while retaining a comparatively simple learning objective.
icml-2024-stochastic-interpolants-with-d.tldr: Data-dependent base-target couplings enable conditional transport models that can still be trained with a simple squared-loss regression objective.

paragraphs: Interactive learning methods must decide what data to collect or where to explore. This paper develops F-design, a criterion for guiding those choices with nonlinear function classes. It generalizes classical G-optimal design and agrees with that established criterion when the function class is linear, providing a connection between the two settings.

The authors call the value of an optimal design its F-condition number. They calculate this value for several nonlinear function classes and give algorithms for constructing designs with a bounded condition number. The work therefore provides both a measure of design quality and procedures for obtaining designs with controlled values of that measure.

The paper applies F-design to confidence-band construction, contextual bandits, model-free reinforcement learning, and active learning. In these four settings, it can be combined with existing approaches as a black-box component. The authors report state-of-the-art results for established problem settings and extensions to new ones. Its broader significance is a reusable design framework that links data collection and exploration across several interactive learning tasks.
icml-2024-the-non-linear-f-design-and-ap.tldr: F-design extends optimal experimental design to nonlinear function classes and supports data collection and exploration across interactive learning tasks.

paragraphs: Difference-in-differences estimates policy effects using a parallel-trends assumption that may fail in practice. Triple difference is increasingly considered as an alternative, but both approaches focus on average effects. This paper asks how to expand that perspective to the distribution of outcomes that would have occurred under a counterfactual policy setting.

The starting point is changes-in-changes, which estimates an entire counterfactual distribution using assumptions about potential-outcome distributions. The authors extend triple difference into this framework and call the resulting method the triple changes estimator. They also state its identification assumptions, specifying the conditions under which the desired counterfactual distribution can be recovered.

The paper empirically evaluates the framework and applies it to Medicaid expansion and children’s preventive care. Its methodological contribution is to connect the additional comparisons of triple difference with the distributional scope of changes-in-changes. This broadens the questions that can be studied beyond an average effect, while keeping identification dependent on the proposed assumptions. The supplied findings describe the framework and application without asserting a particular direction of the policy’s effect.
icml-2024-triple-changes-estimator-for-t.tldr: The triple changes estimator combines triple-difference reasoning with changes-in-changes to identify counterfactual outcome distributions under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: Adam performs well in practice, but standard convergence analyses often yield rates that nonadaptive methods such as stochastic gradient descent can also achieve. That leaves a gap between demonstrating convergence and explaining the value of Adam’s particular components. This paper approaches that gap through online learning.

The authors use a framework in which an online learner selects the updates, or increments, made by an optimizer. This reframes optimizer construction as the problem of designing a good learner for those updates. The central observation is that Adam corresponds to Follow-the-Regularized-Leader, a principled online learning framework, when viewed through this formulation.

Building on that correspondence, the paper studies the benefits of Adam’s components from the online learning perspective. The contribution is an alternative explanation of the algorithm’s structure: its update rules can be understood as parts of a coherent learning procedure. This provides a framework for investigating why those components matter beyond what a generic convergence-rate comparison with stochastic gradient descent reveals.
icml-2024-understanding-adam-optimizer-v.tldr: Viewing optimizer updates as online-learning decisions reveals Adam as a form of Follow-the-Regularized-Leader.

paragraphs: Cardinality sketches compactly represent sets while supporting merges and approximate distinct counts. For queries chosen independently of earlier responses, these randomized structures offer strong guarantees over very large numbers of queries. This paper investigates what happens when responses can influence the construction of later inputs.

The authors give an attack on standard estimators that constructs an adversarial input by post-processing answers to a simple collection of nonadaptive queries. The required collection grows linearly with sketch size k. In experiments with HLL++, the attack used only 4k queries. Its simplicity also suggests possible effectiveness when applied to post-processed natural workloads, although that is presented as a possibility.

The paper further shows that changing the estimator alone cannot remove the vulnerability for known sketch structures: any estimator on those structures can be attacked with a number of queries quadratic in k. This matches a generic upper bound. The results distinguish strong guarantees for nonadaptive querying from the substantially different behavior possible when query responses shape future inputs.
icml-2024-unmasking-vulnerabilities-card.tldr: Cardinality sketches can fail under adaptively constructed inputs, with attacks requiring only linear or quadratic numbers of queries in sketch size.
